sec:
Vote by mail or absentee

Can’t get to your polling place on Election Day? Here is how to vote by mail in New Hampshire, from the state’s own election office and its laws. Checked October 21, 2026.

Ask for your ballot by

Monday, November 2Passed

By mail: the clerk mails ballots for requests received by 12 noon on Monday, November 2, 2026 (the day before the election). In person at the clerk's office: until 5 p.m. on Monday, November 2, 2026. Because the ballot must be back by 5 p.m. on Election Day, ask much sooner if you will mail it. Applications are accepted only within six months before the election. (the law)

Send it back by

Tuesday, November 3Passed

Your ballot must reach your town or city clerk by 5 p.m. on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Ballots that arrive later are not counted. (the law)

The last day to ask for a ballot by mail has passed. You can still vote in person, early or on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3.You can still vote in person on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3. Early voting in person runs through Monday, November 2, 2026. When and where to vote early.

New Hampshire’s own page on voting by mail

At school away from home, in New Hampshire or in another state? What New Hampshire says about students is under Show more.

Who can vote by mail

Yes. State law lets you vote absentee only if: you will be away from your town or city on Election Day; you cannot appear in public that day because of a religious commitment; a disability keeps you from voting in person; or work, including caring for children or adults who need care, keeps you from your polling place for all the hours it is open. (A person held in jail for a misdemeanor or while awaiting trial may also apply.) (the law)

How to ask for a ballot

  • By mail. Fill in the state's absentee ballot application (or a written statement with the same details) and send it to the clerk of your town or city. You must include one of these: a copy of your photo ID, or a notarized signature on the application. Without one, no ballot can be sent. The state's laws provide no online request for most voters. (the law)
  • By fax. For the general election, the application may be faxed to your town or city clerk. It still needs a copy of your photo ID or a notarized signature. (the law)
  • In person. Go to your town or city clerk's office and show your photo ID; the clerk gives you your absentee ballot there until 5 p.m. on Monday, November 2, 2026. (the law)

How to send it back

  • By mail. Seal the inner envelope, sign the statement (affidavit) on it, put it in the outer envelope, add a stamp and mail it to your town or city clerk. (the law)
  • In person. Bring it to your town or city clerk yourself, or have a close family member (spouse, parent, brother or sister, child, grandchild, in-law, stepparent or stepchild) deliver it. A family member delivering it fills in a state form and shows a government photo ID. Nursing home and care facility staff, and a person who helped a voter with a disability, may also deliver within limits. (the law)

What the envelope needs

To get the ballot you must include a copy of your photo ID with the application, have your signature on the application notarized, or show photo ID to the clerk in person. When you return the ballot you sign the statement on the inner envelope; your signature is compared with the one on your application. A person who helps a voter with a disability signs a statement saying so. (the law)

Vote early in person instead

If you qualify to vote absentee, you can get your absentee ballot at your town or city clerk's office until 5 p.m. on Monday, November 2, 2026, and hand your ballot back to the clerk until 5 p.m. on Election Day. (the law)

Students

At school in New Hampshire, away from home

State law says a student may claim as their voting home the New Hampshire town or city where they live while going to school, if it meets the state's rule for a voting home (the one place where you live and mean to keep living for everyday and civic life). State law also says you do not lose your voting home just by being away as a student, and you can have only one voting home. So a student can register where they go to school, or stay registered at home. (the law)

At school in another state, with New Hampshire as home

State law says you do not lose your New Hampshire voting home by being away as a student, and a home lasts until you gain a new one. Under the absentee law, a voter who will be away from their town or city on Election Day may vote absentee. A student from another state who is in New Hampshire only for a temporary purpose and plans to return home does not gain a New Hampshire voting home. (the law)

Military and overseas

Military voters, their families and U.S. citizens overseas use the Federal Post Card Application (FPCA), which counts as New Hampshire's application. Clerks may email absentee ballots only to these voters. A Federal Write-In Absentee Ballot can be used if the regular ballot does not come in time. (the law)

New Hampshire in the Federal Voting Assistance Program’s guide

Good to know

  • Since September 30, 2025, every absentee application needs a copy of your photo ID, a notarized signature, or photo ID shown to the clerk in person.
  • If you are not yet registered and are away from your town, you can register by mail as an absentee voter; registering needs proof of U.S. citizenship, age, home address and identity. Ask your town or city clerk.
  • Ballot tracking: the state's own lookup could not be checked because sos.nh.gov refused our request; ask your town or city clerk whether your ballot has arrived.

How this was checked

  • The Secretary of State's own absentee page (sos.nh.gov) could not be read for this record (it refused an request earlier, and did not answer during the check), so this record is built from the state's election laws as published by the Legislature. Your town or city clerk is the place to confirm forms and hours.
Where this comes from: 3 pages of New Hampshire’s election office, its laws and the federal guide

  2. RSA Chapter 657, Absentee Voting (all sections: 657:6, 657:12, 657:15, 657:17, 657:17-c, 657:22), New Hampshire General Court (the law; read October 21, 2026)
  3. RSA Chapter 654, Voters and Checklists (654:1, 654:2), New Hampshire General Court (the law; read October 21, 2026)

Checked October 21, 2026. Rules and dates can change: New Hampshire’s election office, and your county or local election office, have the final word.

polls:
Polls close no earlier than 7 p.m.; some towns stay open to 8 p.m. Each town sets its opening time. (the law)

Anyone in line when the polls close may still vote.
